title: Two-Way Blade Modeling Method for Structural Redesign of Compressor Blades
contribution: A two-way blade modelling tool (PAR: CAD to interpretable parameters via a NOMAD-solved identification problem; GEN/MSH: parameters to CAD and FE mesh) validated on NASA rotor 37/67 with geometric and dynamic criteria, and used in a 4-variable NOMAD redesign of rotor 37 that improves dynamic clearance by 98 % (pp. 4-5, 15-16, 17-24).
problem_entry: Industrial gap: contact-interaction simulations were never integrated into blade design, and few methods both extract intuitive parameters from an existing (confidential, CAD-only) blade and regenerate its CAD model (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Make an existing blade an optimization starting point: fit the conical-section parameterization to the CAD by DFO (min e(x), bounds, 11 vars, 1500 evals), then run a bound-constrained MADS redesign on 4 stacking variables with dynamic clearance as surrogate objective (pp. 5, 15-16, 23).
assumptions: Input is a CAD model; bounds only; gradients unavailable (profile discretization; 30 s simulation); CAD/mesh failures act as hidden constraints; dynamic clearance assumed a cheap proxy for contact robustness; no convergence hypotheses stated (pp. 4, 16, 23).
proof_devices: none: no theorem or convergence analysis
geometric derivation of the cone-origin formula in the change-of-basis appendix (Eq. 17, p. 27, skimmed)
empirical budget justification: convergence checked on 17 profiles, 1500 evaluations sufficient (p. 16)
inherited acceptance threshold e(x) <= 0.05 from a prior MSc thesis (p. 19)
experiments: Fidelity on NASA rotor 37/67 for n_sec in {2,3,5,9,17} (volume, profile error, 10 natural frequencies, dynamic clearance, contact NFRC; n_sec = 5 best); one default-NOMAD redesign run, 400 evals at ~30 s, 3/400 failures, clearance -0.46 to -0.0089 mm, a-posteriori NFRC amplitude -75 %; no competitor, no replicates (pp. 18-24, 33).
positioning: Extends Batailly's earlier MADS-based blade optimization [20] (planar-tip simplification removed, extraction step added); cites only MADS [36] and NOMAD 3 [39] from the Audet group; does not cite DiscoMads (pp. 3-5, 38).
writing: Engineering framing: states six tool requirements (fidelity, resolution, robustness, interpretability, versatility, efficiency) up front and validates them in Sec. 3 and appendix 5.4; calls the work a proof of concept (pp. 2, 4-5, 17, 33).
limits_future: Fidelity limited by the profile parameterization; aerodynamics excluded; only the first bending mode; future: other blades, other criteria, other modes, and an optimizer handling discontinuous quantities (pp. 22, 24-26).

method_links.note: CAD/mesh generation errors handled as failed simulations by MADS without stopping; 3/400 failures reported; failures reduced at the source by adaptive sewing tolerance and a stress test.
Bounds-only problems; no EB/PB classification; realism enforced by design-space reduction (frozen profiles, quadratic interpolation of sections) rather than constraints.
NOMAD 3.9.1 with default parameters used off the shelf twice: inverse identification (1500 evals) and redesign (400 evals).
Evaluation counts and per-evaluation time reported, but a single run with no competing solver, replication or profiles; the optimizer is a tool.
Uses public NASA rotor 37/67 CAD models; no release of the PAR/GEN/MSH tool or of the dynamic-clearance blackbox is stated.
Names cost (~30 s), unavailable gradient due to discretization, and simulation failures.
14 -> 11 identification variables by reading parameters off data; 4 redesign variables by freezing profiles and interpolating sections.
Reader's inference via card c03: future work names discontinuous quantities, which the same authors' DiscoMads addresses; this paper does not draw the link.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Build the missing blackbox-callable tool to open a new application field to DFO
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two-way parameterizer (PAR/GEN/MSH) built so that redesign of existing industrial blades becomes a blackbox optimization problem; co-authored with a structural-dynamics professor.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: DFO inverse fit seeds DFO redesign
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Bound-constrained NOMAD identification fits parameters to the existing blade; the fitted 5-section model is x0 of the redesign.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fidelity judged on the quantity of interest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Parameterized model validated by geometry, natural frequencies, dynamic clearance, then full contact NFRC, over nested n_sec levels.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: cheap proxy objective, expensive a-posteriori check
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimizer minimizes dynamic clearance only; nonlinear contact simulations run once on initial and optimized designs (75 % amplitude reduction).

transferable: To optimize around an existing design known only as geometry, first fit your parameterization by DFO (data-misfit objective, data-relative x0 and bounds), then start the design optimization from the fitted parameters (pp. 15-17, 22).
Compute every parameter readable directly from the data and remove it from the variable vector (14 -> 11, p. 16).
Keep a redesign low-dimensional and realistic by freezing parameters owned by another discipline and interpolating intermediate sections from a few control sections (4 variables, p. 23).
Justify a fixed evaluation budget by checking convergence on a representative instance set (17 profiles, 1500 evals, p. 16).
Run model-fidelity studies on nested resolution levels (2, 3, 5, 9, 17) with criteria ordered from cheap to strict, ending with the full downstream simulation (pp. 18-22).
Report blackbox failure counts and causes next to the optimization result, and module timings against one simulation's cost (pp. 23, 33).
List the requirements of an optimization-facing model up front and map each to its validation section (pp. 4-5, 17, 33-34).

quotes.text: This algorithm is well-suited for time-consuming simulations and can manage failed simulations without stopping the optimization.

Other performance criteria could be considered, as well as modification of the optimization algorithm to account for special characteristics of contact simulations, such as the presence of discontinuous quantities.
